symptoms: Swelling of the limbs and ventral abdomen
transmission: Mechanically transmitted by biting flies such as Tabanus (horseflies) and Stomoxys (stable flies).
treatment: Administration of specific trypanocidal drugs paired with supportive care and rest.
medicine: Quinapyramine sulfate/chloride, Melarsomine hydrochloride, or Suramin
prevention: Control biting fly populations around water points and treat infected animals promptly.

symptoms: Skin papules and pustules around lips, nose, and eyelids
transmission: Direct contact between infected and healthy camels, scab particles, and contaminated feeding troughs.
treatment: Supportive therapy to prevent secondary bacterial skin and lung infections, along with local lesion cleansing.
medicine: Broad-spectrum injectable antibiotics like Oxytetracycline and topical antiseptic sprays
prevention: Vaccination with attenuated camelpox vaccine and isolation of infected herds.

symptoms: Severe respiratory distress and rapid breathing
Hot painful swelling in the throat and brisket
transmission: Inhalation or ingestion of bacteria triggered by physical stress, long trekking, drought, or overcrowding.
treatment: Immediate systemic antimicrobial therapy combined with anti-inflammatory medication.
medicine: Oxytetracycline, Penicillin-Streptomycin, or Sulfa drugs
prevention: Prophylactic vaccination before stress periods and minimizing hardship during seasonal migrations.

symptoms: Severe itching, biting, and scratching against trees
Hair loss starting at head, neck, and flanks
Open skin sores and secondary bacterial infections
transmission: Direct contact with infested camels or indirect contact via shared trees, saddles, and equipment.
treatment: Systemic injectable antiparasitic drugs combined with topical acaricide washes.
medicine: Ivermectin injection or topical Amitraz/Deltamethrin wash
prevention: Quarantine newly acquired camels and spray herds regularly with approved acaricides.

symptoms: Chronic weight loss and poor growth
Bottle jaw (fluid accumulation under the lower jaw)
transmission: Ingestion of infective larvae from contaminated pastures or vegetation near watering holes.
treatment: Administration of broad-spectrum oral or injectable anthelmintic remedies.
medicine: Ivermectin, Albendazole, or Levamisole
prevention: Strategic deworming at the start and end of rainy seasons and rotational grazing management.

symptoms: Thick exudative crusts and scabs on back and hump
Loss of wool patches leaving raw skin
transmission: Bacterial entry into wet or damaged skin following heavy rainfall or tick bites.
treatment: Systemic antimicrobial injections combined with gentle removal of crusts using antiseptic washes.
medicine: Long-acting Oxytetracycline or Procaine Penicillin
prevention: Control tick infestations and keep animals in dry, clean pens during rainy periods.

symptoms: Sudden death with little or no prior illness
Dark non-clotting blood discharging from nose, mouth, and anus
Rapid bloating of carcass after death
High fever and trembling just before death
Severe swelling of neck and throat area
transmission: Ingestion of persistent bacterial spores from contaminated soil or water during grazing.
treatment: Immediate high-dose antibiotic therapy if caught early, though progression is usually fatal.
medicine: Penicillin G or Oxytetracycline
prevention: Annual vaccination in endemic pasture regions and safe deep burial of unopened carcasses with quicklime.

transmission: Direct contact with infected secretions, respiratory aerosols, saliva, or feces.
treatment: Supportive care including hydration, mouth cleaning with mild antiseptics, and broad-spectrum antibiotics to prevent secondary bacterial infections.
medicine: Oxytetracycline or Penicillin-Streptomycin for secondary infections, plus anti-inflammatory drugs.
prevention: Annual vaccination with live attenuated PPR vaccine and quarantine of newly introduced livestock.

transmission: Inhalation of infectious droplets exhaled by infected goats in close contact.
treatment: Early antimicrobial therapy combined with supportive care before irreversible lung damage occurs.
medicine: Tylosin, Oxytetracycline, or Florfenicol.
prevention: Vaccination with CCPP inactivated vaccine, isolation of sick animals, and avoiding overcrowding.

symptoms: Skin papules and scabs on unwoolled areas
transmission: Direct contact with infected animals, scab material, respiratory droplets, or mechanically by biting insects.
treatment: Symptomatic treatment including wound dressing to prevent fly strike and systemic antibiotics for secondary infections.
medicine: Broad-spectrum antibiotics such as Oxytetracycline and topical antiseptics.
prevention: Vaccination with live attenuated Capripoxvirus vaccine and vector control.

symptoms: High mortality in newborn lambs and kids
transmission: Bites from infected mosquitoes (primarily Aedes and Culex species) following heavy rains.
treatment: Supportive care only; no targeted antiviral treatment is available. Handle carcasses with care due to human zoonotic risk.
medicine: Supportive fluids and anti-inflammatory medications. Avoid invasive procedures due to bleeding risk.
prevention: Vaccination prior to expected rain cycles and mosquito vector control.

symptoms: Sudden death in rapidly growing young animals
transmission: Overgrowth of resident gut bacteria triggered by sudden dietary shifts to high-grain or lush pastures.
treatment: Often rapidly fatal, but early intervention includes clostridial antitoxin, oral antibiotics, and gut motility support.
medicine: Clostridium perfringens type D antitoxin and oral/parenteral Penicillin or Oxytetracycline.
prevention: Vaccination with multivalent clostridial toxoid vaccine and gradual dietary transitions.

symptoms: Fluid accumulation around heart and lungs
transmission: Bites of vector ticks belonging to the genus Amblyomma (bont ticks).
treatment: Early administration of tetracyclines during the febrile stage before severe nervous signs develop.
medicine: Long-acting Oxytetracycline combined with anti-inflammatory drugs like Flunixin meglumine.
prevention: Regular tick control using acaricide dips, sprays, or pour-on formulations.

symptoms: Thick scabs around muzzle and lips
transmission: Direct contact with infected lesions or indirect contact via rough, thorny dryland vegetation.
treatment: Supportive care focused on softening scabs, topical antiseptic application, and palatable soft feed.
medicine: Topical iodine, antiseptic sprays, and systemic broad-spectrum antibiotics for severe secondary infections.
prevention: Vaccination of vulnerable young stock by scarification and isolation of affected animals.

symptoms: Blisters and erosions in interdigital space
Severe lameness and reluctance to walk
transmission: Extremely contagious via direct contact, aerosol transmission, and virus-contaminated equipment or pasture.
treatment: Symptomatic therapy including foot baths, wound care, and provision of soft feed and clean water.
medicine: Topical antiseptics (copper sulfate footbaths, iodine) and systemic antibiotics for secondary infection.
prevention: Vaccination matched to regional viral serotypes, movement restrictions, and strict biosecurity.

transmission: Ingestion of infective L3 larvae present on pasture grasses during damp or rainy periods.
treatment: Targeted anthelmintic deworming based on clinical scoring (e.g. FAMACHA) alongside iron and nutritional support.
medicine: Ivermectin, Albendazole, Levamisole, or Closantel.
prevention: Rotational grazing, selective deworming strategies, and pasture management.

cause: Trypanosoma congolense, Trypanosoma vivax, or Trypanosoma brucei
transmission: Bites from tsetse flies (Glossina spp.) or mechanical transmission by biting flies like Tabanids.
treatment: Administration of trypanocidal drugs combined with good nutrition and stress reduction.
medicine: Diminazene aceturate or Isometamidium chloride.
prevention: Vector control using traps, targets, pyrethroid pour-ons, and prophylactic drug treatment in high-risk zones.

cause: Bacterial pathogens including Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, and E. coli
symptoms: Swollen, warm, or painful udder quarters
Fever and lethargy in acute cases
Reluctance to walk or nurse young
transmission: Poor hygiene during milking, contaminated environment, or direct contact from infected animals
treatment: Intramammary antibiotic infusions and systemic treatment for severe acute cases
medicine: Intramammary penicillin/streptomycin or Cloxacillin combinations, and systemic Oxytetracycline
prevention: Proper milking hygiene, udder washing, post-milking teat dipping, and dry period therapy

symptoms: Crackling feeling under skin when pressed
transmission: Ingestion of bacterial spores from contaminated soil
treatment: Early treatment with high doses of antibiotics, though response is poor once clinical signs are advanced
medicine: Penicillin or Oxytetracycline, along with anti-inflammatory drugs
prevention: Routine vaccination with multi-strain clostridial vaccines

transmission: Direct contact via inhalation of respiratory droplets from infected cattle
treatment: Antibiotic treatment can reduce clinical signs but may leave chronic carrier status
medicine: Tylosin or Oxytetracycline
prevention: Annual vaccination, restricted animal movements, and isolation of affected herds

symptoms: Swollen lymph nodes behind ears and shoulders
Difficulty breathing and frothy nasal discharge
transmission: Transmitted by the brown ear tick (Rhipicephalus appendiculatus)
treatment: Specific antiprotozoal drugs administered early in the disease process
medicine: Buparvaquone and supportive antimicrobial therapy
prevention: Regular tick control using acaricide dips/sprays and vaccination

symptoms: Firm, raised skin nodules all over the body
transmission: Biting insects such as mosquitoes, biting flies, and ticks
treatment: Supportive care focused on wound treatment and treating secondary bacterial infections
medicine: Broad-spectrum antibiotics (Oxytetracycline), anti-inflammatories, and topical antiseptics
prevention: Annual vaccination and insect vector control
